question: A 32-year-old found somnolent after opioid ingestion breathes 6 breaths/min. ABG: PaO2 = 58 mmHg [>80], PaCO2 = 68 mmHg [35-45]. Which of the following best explains his gas abnormalities?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Global underventilation with normal A-a gradient
options.rationale: Correct because depressed alveolar ventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers PaO2 equally producing a normal A-a gradient; the lecture states hypoventilation causes hypoxemia with hypercapnia and normal A-a gradient. A change that would make another option correct would be an increased A-a gradient indicating a diffusion or V/Q problem.

options.text: Low inspired oxygen pressure at altitude
options.rationale: Wrong because high altitude causes low PaO2 with low PaCO2 from hyperventilation; here PaCO2 is elevated. This option would be correct if PaCO2 were low and pH alkalemic due to hyperventilation.

options.text: Impaired alveolar capillary oxygen diffusion
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment typically widens the A-a gradient and often worsens with exercise while PaCO2 is usually normal; this would be correct if DLCO were reduced and A-a gradient increased.

options.text: Marked ventilation perfusion mismatch from COPD
options.rationale: Wrong because V/Q mismatch usually increases the A-a gradient and may not produce marked hypercapnia early; this would be correct if A-a gradient were elevated and supplemental O2 improved PaO2.

options.text: Right to left intrapulmonary shunt unresponsive to O2
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt causes severe A-a widening and poor response to supplemental oxygen while PaCO2 is not typically very high; this would be correct if PaO2 failed to rise with 100% O2 and A-a gradient were very large.

question: A healthy climber at 12,000 ft develops headache and dyspnea. ABG: PaO2 = 55 mmHg [>80], PaCO2 = 28 mmHg [35-45], pH = 7.50 [7.35-7.45]. Which mechanism best accounts for these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Reduced ambient pressure causing hyperventilation
options.rationale: Correct because decreased barometric pressure lowers inspired PO2 producing hypoxemia that triggers peripheral chemoreceptor–driven hyperventilation, lowering PaCO2 and causing respiratory alkalosis as described for high altitude in the lecture. If PaCO2 were high instead, hypoventilation would be more likely.

options.text: Central respiratory depression from sedative overdose
options.rationale: Wrong because central depression causes hypoventilation with elevated PaCO2 and respiratory acidosis; this would be correct if PaCO2 were high and pH acidotic.

options.text: Alveolar capillary membrane thickening from fibrosis
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment usually yields a widened A-a gradient and normal or low PaCO2; this would be correct if DLCO were reduced and A-a gradient increased.

options.text: Large intrapulmonary right to left shunt
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt produces severe hypoxemia that responds poorly to supplemental oxygen and typically shows a large A-a gradient; this would be correct if oxygen therapy failed to raise PaO2.

options.text: Regional low ventilation relative to perfusion
options.rationale: Wrong because V/Q mismatch usually increases the A-a gradient and does not typically cause hypocapnia from hyperventilation; this would be correct if A-a gradient were elevated and oxygen corrected PaO2.

question: Which single laboratory pattern from the lecture indicates hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Low PaO2 with elevated PaCO2 and normal A-a
options.rationale: Correct because hypoventilation lowers PAO2 and PaO2 while raising PaCO2 with little change in A-a gradient; the lecture emphasizes hypoventilation produces hypoxemia with hypercapnia and normal A-a. If A-a were widened, diffusion or V/Q problems would be implicated.

options.text: Low PaO2 with low PaCO2 and widened A-a
options.rationale: Wrong because low PaCO2 with widened A-a suggests high altitude or V/Q mismatch with compensatory hyperventilation; this would be correct if the clinical context were ascent to altitude or V/Q mismatch with hyperventilation.

options.text: Low PaO2 with normal PaCO2 and normal A-a
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment or shunt typically widens the A-a gradient; this would be correct only if an unusual global hypoxic exposure lowered inspired PO2 without affecting CO2.

options.text: Low PaO2 with normal PaCO2 and widened A-a
options.rationale: Wrong because this pattern fits diffusion impairment or V/Q mismatch rather than normal A-a; it would be correct if DLCO were reduced or supplemental O2 response clarified the cause.

options.text: Low PaO2 with elevated PaCO2 and widened A-a
options.rationale: Wrong because combined hypercapnia and widened A-a suggests mixed processes; this would be correct if both hypoventilation and V/Q mismatch or shunt were present.

question: A patient with restrictive lung disease has PaO2 = 60 mmHg [>80], PaCO2 = 34 mmHg [35-45], and worsening desaturation with exercise. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Impaired oxygen diffusion across thickened membrane
options.rationale: Correct because interstitial thickening slows O2 equilibration causing widened A-a gradient and exercise-induced worsening; the lecture lists fibrosis and interstitial edema as diffusion impairment causes with increased DLCO noted as abnormal. If DLCO were normal and oxygen improved fully, V/Q mismatch would be more likely.

options.text: Global hypoventilation from neuromuscular weakness
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation causes hypercapnia rather than low PaCO2; this would be correct if PaCO2 were elevated and A-a gradient normal.

options.text: High altitude exposure with compensatory hyperventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because altitude causes low PaCO2 from hyperventilation and not exercise-limited diffusion worsening; this would be correct if PaCO2 were low and A-a gradient normal.

options.text: Right to left pulmonary shunt from atelectasis
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt typically shows poor response to supplemental oxygen and large A-a gradient; this would be correct if oxygen therapy failed to raise PaO2 significantly.

options.text: Regional low ventilation relative to perfusion
options.rationale: Wrong because V/Q mismatch may improve with supplemental oxygen and does not characteristically worsen only with exercise due to diffusion limitation; this would be correct if oxygen corrected PaO2 and DLCO were normal.

question: Which of the following causes listed in the lecture most directly produces a widened A-a gradient but usually normal PaCO2 at rest?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Ventilation perfusion mismatch from pneumonia
options.rationale: Correct because low V/Q regions mix with normal blood increasing the A-a gradient while PaCO2 often remains normal due to compensation by healthy regions; the lecture lists pneumonia as a common low V/Q cause. If PaCO2 were elevated, hypoventilation would be implicated instead.

options.text: Global hypoventilation from opioid overdose
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation produces a normal A-a gradient with elevated PaCO2; this would be correct if A-a were normal and PaCO2 high.

options.text: Reduced inspired oxygen at high altitude
options.rationale: Wrong because altitude lowers PaO2 with a normal A-a gradient and low PaCO2 from hyperventilation; this would be correct if PaCO2 were low and A-a normal.

options.text: Right to left shunt from severe atelectasis
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt also widens A-a but often shows poor response to supplemental oxygen; this would be correct if oxygen therapy failed to raise PaO2 markedly.

options.text: Decreased alveolar surface area from emphysema
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema can cause diffusion limitation and V/Q mismatch with variable PaCO2; this would be correct if DLCO were reduced and exercise worsened hypoxemia.

question: A patient with ARDS has PaO2 = 55 mmHg [>80] while receiving 100% oxygen. Which mechanism from the lecture best explains persistent hypoxemia despite maximal inspired oxygen?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Right to left intrapulmonary shunting of blood
options.rationale: Correct because blood bypasses ventilated alveoli and mixes venous blood into arterial circulation, so supplemental oxygen cannot fully correct PaO2; the lecture emphasizes shunt physiology and poor response to O2. If shunt fraction were small, oxygen would improve PaO2.

options.text: Global hypoventilation with elevated PaCO2
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation would raise PaCO2 and typically respond to increased ventilation rather than fail with 100% O2; this would be correct if PaCO2 were high and A-a normal.

options.text: High altitude causing low inspired oxygen tension
options.rationale: Wrong because high altitude hypoxemia improves with supplemental oxygen and shows low PaCO2 from hyperventilation; this would be correct if PaCO2 were low and oxygen corrected PaO2.

options.text: Isolated diffusion impairment across alveolar membrane
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion defects usually improve with high FiO2 and are exercise-sensitive; this would be correct if DLCO were reduced and oxygen partially corrected PaO2.

options.text: Mild V/Q mismatch correctable with oxygen therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because mild V/Q mismatch typically responds to supplemental oxygen; this would be correct if PaO2 rose substantially with increased FiO2.

question: Which diagnostic pattern from the lecture differentiates diffusion impairment from right-to-left shunt?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Widened A-a gradient with PaO2 improving on O2
options.rationale: Correct because diffusion impairment and low V/Q typically show widened A-a but improve with supplemental oxygen, whereas true shunt does not; the lecture uses response to O2 to distinguish these. If PaO2 failed to rise with O2, a shunt would be more likely.

options.text: Normal A-a gradient with elevated PaCO2 at rest
options.rationale: Wrong because that pattern indicates hypoventilation rather than diffusion or shunt; this would be correct if alveolar ventilation were globally reduced.

options.text: Widened A-a gradient with no PaO2 change on O2
options.rationale: Wrong because lack of response to oxygen indicates shunt rather than diffusion impairment; this would be correct if shunt fraction were large and oxygen failed to raise PaO2.

options.text: Low PaO2 with low PaCO2 and normal A-a gradient
options.rationale: Wrong because low PaCO2 with normal A-a suggests high altitude rather than diffusion impairment; this would be correct if the patient had reduced inspired oxygen tension.

options.text: Elevated PaCO2 with widened A-a gradient
options.rationale: Wrong because combined hypercapnia and widened A-a suggests mixed pathology; this would be correct if both hypoventilation and V/Q mismatch or shunt coexisted.

question: A 72-year-old smoker with chronic cough has PaO2 = 58 mmHg [>80], PaCO2 = 41 mmHg [35-45], PAO2 = 100 mmHg [>100], and DLCO normal. Supplemental oxygen improves PaO2. Which cause from the lecture best fits?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Low ventilation perfusion ratio from COPD
options.rationale: Correct because V/Q mismatch from COPD widens the A-a gradient while DLCO can be normal and oxygen typically improves PaO2; the lecture lists COPD as a common low V/Q cause. If DLCO were low and oxygen response limited, diffusion impairment or shunt would be more likely.

options.text: Global hypoventilation from central depression
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation would show elevated PaCO2 and normal A-a; this would be correct if PaCO2 were high and PAO2 low by the same amount.

options.text: High altitude exposure with compensatory hyperventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because altitude causes low PaCO2 and normal A-a gradient; this would be correct if PaCO2 were low and PAO2 reduced due to low barometric pressure.

options.text: Right to left intracardiac shunt unresponsive to oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt typically does not correct with supplemental oxygen; this would be correct if oxygen failed to raise PaO2 despite high FiO2.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar capillary membrane thickening
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment usually reduces DLCO; this would be correct if DLCO were decreased and exercise worsened hypoxemia.

question: Which physiologic statement from the lecture correctly contrasts hypoventilation and low V/Q mismatch?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Hypoventilation lowers PaO2 and raises PaCO2 with normal A-a
options.rationale: Correct because hypoventilation reduces alveolar ventilation globally causing parallel decreases in PAO2 and increases in PACO2 with a normal A-a gradient; the lecture explicitly contrasts this with low V/Q. If only some alveoli were affected, A-a would widen indicating V/Q mismatch.

options.text: Low V/Q lowers PaO2 and lowers PaCO2 with normal A-a
options.rationale: Wrong because low V/Q usually widens the A-a gradient and PaCO2 is often normal due to compensation; this would be correct only in a rare global hyperventilation scenario.

options.text: Hypoventilation widens A-a gradient and lowers PaCO2
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation does not widen A-a and raises PaCO2; this would be correct only if there were concurrent diffusion impairment.

options.text: Low V/Q narrows A-a gradient and raises PaCO2
options.rationale: Wrong because low V/Q widens, not narrows, the A-a gradient and does not necessarily raise PaCO2; this would be correct if global hypoventilation coexisted.

options.text: Hypoventilation increases DLCO and widens A-a gradient
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation does not increase DLCO nor widen A-a; this would be correct only with superimposed diffusion pathology.

question: A patient breathes 100% oxygen and arterial PaO2 rises only modestly. The lecture shows that increasing shunt fraction reduces arterial PO2 despite high FiO2. Which physiologic principle explains this?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Admixture of venous blood lowers arterial oxygen tension
options.rationale: Correct because mixing nonoxygenated venous blood with oxygenated arterial blood reduces overall oxygen content and PaO2 even when arterial blood is superoxygenated; the lecture demonstrates admixture calculations showing reduced PaO2 after mixing. If no venous admixture occurred, PaO2 would reach near alveolar values with 100% O2.

options.text: Increased FiO2 always normalizes PaCO2 and PaO2
options.rationale: Wrong because FiO2 raises PAO2 but cannot correct PaO2 when large shunt fractions mix venous blood; this would be correct only if no shunt were present.

options.text: Diffusion limitation prevents any rise in PaO2 on oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion defects usually improve with high FiO2; this would be correct only in extreme membrane failure with no surface area for gas exchange.

options.text: Hyperventilation induced by oxygen lowers PaO2
options.rationale: Wrong because hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 and can raise PAO2 indirectly; it does not explain poor PaO2 rise with 100% O2 in shunt. This would be correct only if ventilation decreased alveolar oxygen delivery.

options.text: High V/Q regions steal blood flow reducing PaO2
options.rationale: Wrong because high V/Q reduces perfusion but does not explain failure of PaO2 to rise with 100% O2 in shunt; this would be correct if perfusion redistribution caused significant dead space physiology.

question: A patient with pulmonary edema has hypoxemia that improves with supplemental oxygen. According to the lecture, which primary mechanism most likely causes this improvement?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Correction of low V/Q regions by increasing PAO2
options.rationale: Correct because supplemental oxygen raises alveolar PO2 in poorly ventilated regions, improving oxygen content of blood from low V/Q units; the lecture notes that oxygen corrects hypoxemia from V/Q mismatch. If the problem were a large shunt, oxygen would not correct PaO2 effectively.

options.text: Reversal of alveolar capillary membrane thickening
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not reverse structural membrane thickening; this would be correct only if the membrane pathology were transient and resolved.

options.text: Elimination of venous admixture from intracardiac shunt
options.rationale: Wrong because supplemental oxygen cannot eliminate anatomic shunt admixture; this would be correct only if the shunt were surgically corrected.

options.text: Suppression of central respiratory drive to lower PaCO2
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not suppress drive to lower PaCO2 in a way that corrects hypoxemia from edema; this would be correct only if hyperventilation were causing the problem.

options.text: Redistribution of pulmonary blood flow to dead space
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not beneficially redistribute flow to dead space; this would be correct only if perfusion changes improved matching, which is unlikely.

question: A patient has PAO2 = 100 mmHg [>100], PaO2 = 70 mmHg [>80], PaCO2 = 40 mmHg [35-45], and DLCO is low. Which cause from the lecture best explains these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Diffusion impairment from reduced alveolar surface area
options.rationale: Correct because a low DLCO with a large A-a gradient and normal PaCO2 indicates impaired O2 transfer across the alveolar-capillary membrane; the lecture lists low DLCO as a key lab for diffusion impairment. If DLCO were normal and oxygen corrected fully, V/Q mismatch would be more likely.

options.text: Global hypoventilation causing elevated PaCO2
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation would raise PaCO2 and produce a normal A-a gradient; this would be correct if PaCO2 were high and PAO2 decreased by the same amount.

options.text: High altitude with compensatory hyperventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because altitude lowers PAO2 and PaO2 with low PaCO2; this would be correct if PAO2 were low and PaCO2 decreased.

options.text: Right to left shunt unresponsive to supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt typically shows poor oxygen response but does not necessarily lower DLCO; this would be correct if oxygen failed to raise PaO2 despite high FiO2.

options.text: Low V/Q mismatch with normal DLCO
options.rationale: Wrong because low V/Q often has normal DLCO and improves with oxygen; this would be correct if DLCO were normal and PaO2 rose with supplemental oxygen.

question: Which clinical intervention from the lecture is expected to rapidly reverse hypoxemia caused by opioid-induced respiratory depression?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Administer opioid antagonist and support ventilation
options.rationale: Correct because reversing CNS depression with naloxone and improving alveolar ventilation corrects PaCO2 and PaO2; the lecture notes rapid improvement with naloxone and oxygen in hypoventilation. If the cause were shunt, antagonists would not help.

options.text: Provide high flow oxygen only without ventilation support
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen alone corrects PaO2 but does not address hypercapnia from hypoventilation; this would be correct only as a temporizing measure if ventilation were adequate.

options.text: Begin diuretics to reduce interstitial edema
options.rationale: Wrong because diuretics treat pulmonary edema and diffusion problems, not opioid-induced hypoventilation; this would be correct if pulmonary edema were the primary cause.

options.text: Perform immediate surgical closure of intracardiac shunt
options.rationale: Wrong because intracardiac shunt is not the cause here; this would be correct only if anatomic R-L shunt were documented and causing hypoxemia.

options.text: Start bronchodilators for reversible airway obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchodilators treat obstructive V/Q mismatch, not central hypoventilation from opioids; this would be correct if bronchospasm were present.

question: A patient with interstitial lung disease has normal PaCO2 at rest but marked desaturation on exertion. According to the lecture, which physiologic property explains exercise-induced worsening?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Limited oxygen diffusion time during increased cardiac output
options.rationale: Correct because exercise shortens capillary transit time and diffusion-limited O2 transfer across thickened membranes worsens hypoxemia; the lecture states diffusion impairment worsens with exercise. If capillary transit time remained long, exercise would not worsen diffusion-limited hypoxemia.

options.text: Global hypoventilation reducing alveolar ventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation causes hypercapnia and is not exercise-specific; this would be correct if minute ventilation decreased during exertion.

options.text: High altitude exposure lowering inspired oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because altitude affects inspired PO2 regardless of exercise and causes hypocapnia from hyperventilation; this would be correct if the patient were at altitude.

options.text: Acute intracardiac shunt formation during exercise
options.rationale: Wrong because intracardiac shunts are structural and not typically exercise-induced; this would be correct if a dynamic shunt developed.

options.text: Bronchospasm causing reversible airway obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchospasm causes V/Q mismatch and wheeze, not isolated diffusion limitation; this would be correct if obstructive symptoms and response to bronchodilators were present.

question: Which of the following lecture-derived lab constellations indicates a primary diffusion impairment rather than V/Q mismatch?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: High A-a gradient, low DLCO, PaCO2 normal
options.rationale: Correct because diffusion impairment produces a widened A-a gradient, reduced DLCO, and usually normal PaCO2 at rest; the lecture lists these as key labs for diffusion impairment. If DLCO were normal and oxygen corrected PaO2, V/Q mismatch would be favored.

options.text: High A-a gradient, normal DLCO, PaCO2 elevated
options.rationale: Wrong because elevated PaCO2 suggests hypoventilation and normal DLCO argues against diffusion impairment; this would be correct if global hypoventilation coexisted with V/Q issues.

options.text: Normal A-a gradient, low DLCO, PaCO2 low
options.rationale: Wrong because low DLCO with normal A-a is inconsistent; this would be correct only in rare measurement error or mixed pathology.

options.text: Normal A-a gradient, normal DLCO, PaCO2 elevated
options.rationale: Wrong because this pattern indicates hypoventilation rather than diffusion impairment; this would be correct if alveolar ventilation were reduced.

options.text: High A-a gradient, normal DLCO, PaCO2 normal
options.rationale: Wrong because normal DLCO with widened A-a suggests V/Q mismatch or shunt rather than diffusion impairment; this would be correct if oxygen corrected PaO2.

question: A patient with pneumonia has hypoxemia that corrects with supplemental oxygen. The lecture lists several causes of low V/Q. Which listed cause best matches this clinical response?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Regional alveolar hypoventilation from lobar consolidation
options.rationale: Correct because pneumonia causes localized low V/Q units where supplemental oxygen increases PAO2 and improves arterial oxygenation; the lecture lists pneumonia as a common low V/Q cause that responds to oxygen. If consolidation produced complete alveolar collapse with shunt physiology, oxygen might not correct PaO2.

options.text: Global hypoventilation from opioid intoxication
options.rationale: Wrong because global hypoventilation causes hypercapnia and a normal A-a gradient; this would be correct if PaCO2 were elevated and oxygen response limited.

options.text: High altitude exposure with low inspired PO2
options.rationale: Wrong because altitude hypoxemia shows low PaCO2 and normal A-a gradient; this would be correct if the patient had recent ascent to high altitude.

options.text: Diffuse interstitial fibrosis causing diffusion block
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment may improve with oxygen but is characterized by low DLCO and exercise worsening; this would be correct if DLCO were reduced and A-a gradient large.

options.text: Large intracardiac right to left shunt
options.rationale: Wrong because anatomic shunts often fail to correct with supplemental oxygen; this would be correct if oxygen produced minimal PaO2 change.

question: A patient with severe kyphoscoliosis develops daytime hypoxemia with PaO2 = 60 mmHg [>80] and PaCO2 = 55 mmHg [35-45]. Based on the lecture, which mechanism is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Chest wall restriction causing chronic hypoventilation
options.rationale: Correct because chest wall disorders like kyphoscoliosis reduce alveolar ventilation leading to hypercapnia and hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient; the lecture lists chest wall disorders under hypoventilation causes. If A-a were widened instead, V/Q mismatch or diffusion impairment would be considered.

options.text: High altitude residence causing low inspired oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because altitude causes hypocapnia from hyperventilation, not hypercapnia; this would be correct if PaCO2 were low and the patient had recent ascent.

options.text: Primary diffusion impairment from interstitial disease
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment usually does not cause marked hypercapnia at rest; this would be correct if DLCO were low and A-a gradient widened.

options.text: Right to left pulmonary shunt from atelectasis
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt often shows poor oxygen response and not necessarily hypercapnia; this would be correct if oxygen failed to raise PaO2.

options.text: Obstructive airway disease causing high V/Q regions
options.rationale: Wrong because obstructive disease typically causes V/Q mismatch with variable PaCO2; this would be correct if A-a gradient were elevated and oxygen improved PaO2.

question: Which single measurement from the lecture is most useful to quantify the severity of oxygenation impairment in ARDS?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: PaO2 to FiO2 ratio (P over F) value
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture introduces the PaO2/FiO2 (P/F) ratio as the Horowitz index to assess lung function and ARDS severity with defined cutoffs for mild, moderate, and severe ARDS. If only PaO2 were known without FiO2, severity quantification would be incomplete.

options.text: Alveolar arterial oxygen gradient alone
options.rationale: Wrong because A-a gradient is informative but P/F ratio directly quantifies oxygenation relative to FiO2 for ARDS staging; this would be correct only as supplemental information.

options.text: DLCO measurement at rest
options.rationale: Wrong because DLCO assesses diffusion capacity rather than global oxygenation severity in ARDS; this would be correct if diffusion impairment were the primary concern.

options.text: Mixed venous oxygen saturation alone
options.rationale: Wrong because mixed venous O2 reflects systemic extraction and cardiac output, not ARDS oxygenation severity; this would be correct if global delivery issues were suspected.

options.text: PaCO2 value without FiO2 context
options.rationale: Wrong because PaCO2 indicates ventilation status but not oxygenation severity relative to FiO2; this would be correct only for ventilatory failure assessment.

question: A patient with pulmonary embolism often has regions with high V/Q. According to the lecture, how does high V/Q affect arterial oxygenation and PaCO2?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Perfusion reduced relative to ventilation causing dead space
options.rationale: Correct because pulmonary embolism reduces perfusion to ventilated alveoli creating high V/Q units and physiologic dead space; the lecture lists pulmonary embolism as a high V/Q cause. This tends to impair CO2 elimination less than oxygenation but increases dead space ventilation.

options.text: Ventilation reduced relative to perfusion causing hypoxemia
options.rationale: Wrong because that describes low V/Q, not high V/Q; this would be correct for pneumonia or COPD causing low ventilation.

options.text: Global hypoventilation raising PaCO2 and lowering PaO2
options.rationale: Wrong because global hypoventilation affects all alveoli and raises PaCO2; this would be correct if minute ventilation were reduced.

options.text: Right to left shunt mixing venous blood into arterial blood
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt is perfusion without ventilation (V/Q = 0), not high V/Q; this would be correct if alveoli were collapsed and unventilated.

options.text: Diffusion limitation across thickened alveolar membrane
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion limitation is a membrane problem rather than perfusion reduction; this would be correct if DLCO were low and exercise worsened hypoxemia.

question: A patient with severe pneumonia has an A-a gradient that is markedly increased. According to the lecture, which additional test result would best distinguish low V/Q from true shunt?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Response of PaO2 to supplemental oxygen therapy
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states that low V/Q improves with supplemental oxygen while true right-to-left shunt does not, making oxygen response the key distinguishing test. If PaO2 fails to rise with high FiO2, shunt is likely.

options.text: Measurement of PaCO2 during quiet breathing
options.rationale: Wrong because PaCO2 helps identify hypoventilation but does not reliably distinguish V/Q mismatch from shunt; this would be correct only if hypercapnia suggested global ventilation failure.

options.text: DLCO measurement at rest
options.rationale: Wrong because DLCO differentiates diffusion impairment from other causes but not V/Q mismatch versus shunt; this would be correct if diffusion impairment were suspected.

options.text: Chest radiograph showing cardiomegaly
options.rationale: Wrong because cardiomegaly does not distinguish V/Q mismatch from shunt; this would be correct only if intracardiac shunt were suspected on imaging.

options.text: Arterial lactate concentration measurement
options.rationale: Wrong because lactate reflects tissue perfusion and anaerobic metabolism, not the pulmonary gas exchange pattern; this would be correct only if systemic hypoperfusion were present.

question: A patient with emphysema has reduced alveolar surface area. Based on the lecture, which gas exchange abnormality is most expected?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Decreased DLCO with widened A-a gradient and hypoxemia
options.rationale: Correct because emphysema reduces surface area for gas exchange lowering DLCO and producing hypoxemia with an increased A-a gradient; the lecture lists decreased surface area as a diffusion impairment cause. If DLCO were normal, V/Q mismatch would be more likely.

options.text: Normal DLCO with normal A-a gradient and hypercapnia
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema typically lowers DLCO and widens A-a; this would be correct only in early disease without diffusion loss.

options.text: Marked improvement of PaO2 with 100% oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema-related diffusion limitation may improve with oxygen but not always markedly; this would be correct if diffusion limitation were minimal.

options.text: Immediate normalization of PaO2 after bronchodilator
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchodilators may improve airflow but do not fully correct diffusion-limited hypoxemia; this would be correct if airway obstruction were the sole cause.

options.text: Low PaO2 with very low PaCO2 from hyperventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema does not typically cause hypocapnia; this would be correct only if the patient hyperventilated for another reason.

question: A patient with suspected hypoxemia has PaO2 = 55 mmHg [>80] and PaCO2 = 40 mmHg [35-45]. The lecture emphasizes the first step in analysis. What is that initial action?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Construct alveolar and arterial gas schematic diagram
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture repeatedly instructs to 'make the picture'—draw alveolar, end-capillary, and arterial compartments to visualize PAO2, PaO2, and PaCO2 relationships as the first diagnostic step. If the diagram shows normal A-a, hypoventilation or altitude are considered next.

options.text: Immediately start broad spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Wrong because empiric antibiotics are a treatment decision not the initial diagnostic step for hypoxemia analysis; this would be correct only if clinical infection evidence existed.

options.text: Order an immediate DLCO measurement before ABG
options.rationale: Wrong because ABG and schematic analysis guide initial differentiation; DLCO is useful later to distinguish diffusion impairment. This would be correct if diffusion impairment were strongly suspected after initial analysis.

options.text: Assume right to left shunt without further testing
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt must be differentiated from other causes using A-a gradient and oxygen response; this would be correct only if oxygen failed to raise PaO2 and A-a was very large.

options.text: Begin noninvasive ventilation without evaluation
options.rationale: Wrong because ventilation support may be needed but diagnostic evaluation should guide therapy; this would be correct if the patient were in respiratory failure requiring immediate support.

question: A patient with severe ARDS has a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 80. According to the lecture's Horowitz index categories, how is this classified?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Severe acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines P/F ratio <100 as severe ARDS on the Horowitz index. If the ratio were 150, it would be classified as moderate ARDS instead.

options.text: Mild acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.rationale: Wrong because mild ARDS corresponds to P/F 200–300; this would be correct only if the ratio fell within that range.

options.text: Normal oxygenation for healthy lungs
options.rationale: Wrong because normal P/F is 500–600; this would be correct only with a much higher PaO2 or lower FiO2.

options.text: Moderate acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.rationale: Wrong because moderate ARDS corresponds to P/F 100–200; this would be correct only if the ratio were between those values.

options.text: Hypoventilation related respiratory failure
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation is characterized by elevated PaCO2 and normal A-a gradient, not P/F categorization; this would be correct if PaCO2 were high and A-a normal.

question: A patient with cyanotic congenital heart disease has an intracardiac right-to-left shunt. Based on the lecture, which statement about supplemental oxygen response is correct?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Supplemental oxygen produces minimal PaO2 improvement
options.rationale: Correct because anatomic R-L shunts mix nonoxygenated venous blood into arterial circulation so increasing FiO2 has limited effect on arterial PaO2; the lecture emphasizes poor oxygen response in shunt. If the shunt were small or intermittent, oxygen might raise PaO2 more.

options.text: Supplemental oxygen fully normalizes PaO2 rapidly
options.rationale: Wrong because shunts do not typically normalize PaO2 with oxygen; this would be correct only if hypoxemia were due to low V/Q or altitude.

options.text: Supplemental oxygen always lowers PaCO2 markedly
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen affects PaO2 more than PaCO2; PaCO2 changes depend on ventilation, not FiO2. This would be correct only if oxygen altered respiratory drive significantly.

options.text: Supplemental oxygen converts shunt physiology to V/Q mismatch
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not change anatomic shunt into V/Q mismatch; this would be correct only if the underlying anatomy changed.

options.text: Supplemental oxygen increases DLCO in shunted blood
options.rationale: Wrong because DLCO measures diffusion capacity and is not increased by oxygen in the presence of shunt; this would be correct only if membrane diffusion improved.

question: A patient presents with daytime somnolence, obesity, and chronic hypoxemia. The lecture lists obesity hypoventilation syndrome among causes. Which gas pattern is most consistent with this syndrome?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Elevated PaCO2 with low PaO2 and normal A-a gradient
options.rationale: Correct because obesity hypoventilation causes inadequate alveolar ventilation leading to hypercapnia and hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient as described under hypoventilation causes. If A-a were widened, additional V/Q or diffusion pathology would be suspected.

options.text: Low PaCO2 with low PaO2 and widened A-a gradient
options.rationale: Wrong because low PaCO2 suggests hyperventilation or altitude, not hypoventilation; this would be correct if the patient were at high altitude.

options.text: Normal PaCO2 with low PaO2 and low DLCO
options.rationale: Wrong because low DLCO indicates diffusion impairment rather than obesity hypoventilation; this would be correct if DLCO were measured low.

options.text: Low PaO2 with poor response to supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because poor oxygen response suggests shunt; this would be correct if oxygen failed to raise PaO2 despite high FiO2.

options.text: Elevated PaCO2 with high DLCO and normal A-a
options.rationale: Wrong because DLCO is unrelated to hypoventilation and would not be elevated; this would be correct only with measurement error or unusual physiology.

question: A patient with severe pneumonia has mixed venous PO2 = 40 mmHg [>40] and arterial PaO2 = 50 mmHg [>80]. The lecture demonstrates admixture calculations. Which factor most directly determines the resulting arterial PaO2 after admixture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Oxygen content of arterial and venous blood before mixing
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture shows that after admixture the oxygen content (mL/dL) of arterial and venous blood determines the mixed PaO2; superoxygenated arterial blood mixed with venous blood lowers overall PaO2 based on content. If venous content were higher, the resulting PaO2 would be higher.

options.text: Alveolar ventilation in unaffected lung regions only
options.rationale: Wrong because while unaffected regions contribute oxygenated blood, the admixture outcome depends on content of both streams; this would be correct only if venous admixture were negligible.

options.text: Total cardiac output irrespective of shunt fraction
options.rationale: Wrong because cardiac output alone does not determine PaO2 without considering shunt fraction and oxygen content; this would be correct only if shunt fraction were constant.

options.text: PaCO2 value in mixed venous blood
options.rationale: Wrong because CO2 content influences acid-base but admixture PaO2 depends primarily on O2 content; this would be correct only if CO2 affected hemoglobin affinity significantly.

options.text: FiO2 delivered to the patient regardless of shunt
options.rationale: Wrong because FiO2 raises arterial oxygen only in ventilated units; with significant shunt, FiO2 effect is limited. This would be correct only if shunt fraction were minimal.

question: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome develops rising PaCO2 and falling PaO2. According to the lecture, which immediate management step addresses the primary pathophysiology?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Initiate ventilatory support to restore alveolar ventilation
options.rationale: Correct because neuromuscular weakness causes hypoventilation with hypercapnia and hypoxemia; mechanical ventilation or noninvasive support restores alveolar ventilation and corrects PaCO2 and PaO2 as the lecture recommends correcting the primary cause. If the problem were diffusion impairment, ventilatory support alone would be less effective.

options.text: Administer high dose corticosteroids to reduce inflammation
options.rationale: Wrong because corticosteroids do not acutely reverse neuromuscular respiratory failure; this would be correct only if an inflammatory lung process causing diffusion impairment were primary.

options.text: Give 100% oxygen without ventilatory assistance
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen alone corrects PaO2 transiently but does not address hypercapnia from hypoventilation; this would be correct only as a temporizing measure if ventilation were adequate.

options.text: Perform urgent thoracentesis to remove pleural fluid
options.rationale: Wrong because pleural effusion removal treats restrictive mechanics but not neuromuscular failure; this would be correct if large effusion were causing hypoventilation.

options.text: Start bronchodilators to relieve airway obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchodilators do not treat neuromuscular weakness; this would be correct if bronchospasm were the cause of hypoxemia.

question: A patient with interstitial pulmonary fibrosis has PaO2 = 65 mmHg [>80] at rest and marked desaturation with exercise. The lecture indicates supplemental oxygen improves resting PaO2. Which cellular-level change most directly explains the benefit of supplemental oxygen in diffusion impairment?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increase alveolar PO2 gradient driving diffusion into blood
options.rationale: Correct because raising alveolar PO2 increases the partial pressure gradient across a thickened membrane, enhancing O2 diffusion into capillary blood despite impaired transfer; the lecture notes supplemental oxygen improves hypoxemia in diffusion impairment. If membrane thickness remained prohibitive, oxygen benefit would be limited.

options.text: Directly thin the alveolar capillary membrane structure
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not reverse structural thickening; this would be correct only if a therapy reduced fibrosis acutely.

options.text: Increase hemoglobin concentration to carry more oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because supplemental oxygen increases dissolved and bound O2 but does not change hemoglobin mass; this would be correct if transfusion increased hemoglobin.

options.text: Reduce pulmonary capillary blood flow to prolong transit time
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not reduce perfusion to increase transit time; this would be correct only if cardiac output were lowered pharmacologically.

options.text: Shift oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen therapy does not intentionally shift the curve right; this would be correct only if factors like acidosis or increased temperature altered affinity.

question: A patient with suspected right-to-left intrapulmonary shunt has PaO2 that fails to rise with 100% oxygen. The lecture suggests which next diagnostic or management step is most informative?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Perform contrast echocardiography to detect intracardiac shunt
options.rationale: Correct because if oxygen fails to correct PaO2, distinguishing intracardiac from intrapulmonary shunt is important; contrast echo can identify intracardiac shunts, aligning with the lecture's emphasis on shunt evaluation. If contrast echo is negative, intrapulmonary shunt or severe V/Q mismatch should be considered.

options.text: Increase FiO2 further beyond 100 percent
options.rationale: Wrong because FiO2 cannot exceed 100% in practice and oxygen already failed to correct PaO2; this would be correct only in theoretical models.

options.text: Administer bronchodilator to open collapsed alveoli
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchodilators do not correct anatomic shunts; this would be correct if reversible airway obstruction caused low V/Q.

options.text: Start empiric antibiotics for presumed pneumonia
options.rationale: Wrong because antibiotics treat infection but do not immediately clarify shunt physiology; this would be correct if clinical infection evidence existed.

options.text: Measure DLCO to confirm diffusion impairment
options.rationale: Wrong because DLCO helps identify diffusion problems but not shunt; this would be correct if diffusion impairment were suspected after oxygen response testing.

question: A postoperative patient develops sudden hypoxemia with PaO2 = 60 mmHg [>80] and PaCO2 = 38 mmHg [35-45]. The lecture lists pulmonary embolism as a high V/Q cause. Which immediate physiologic change best explains the hypoxemia in pulmonary embolism?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Loss of perfusion to ventilated alveoli increasing dead space
options.rationale: Correct because pulmonary embolism reduces perfusion to ventilated alveoli creating high V/Q units and physiologic dead space, impairing effective gas exchange and causing hypoxemia as the lecture describes. If large areas became completely unperfused, CO2 elimination might be affected differently.

options.text: Global hypoventilation lowering alveolar oxygen tension
options.rationale: Wrong because global hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and produces a normal A-a gradient; this would be correct if minute ventilation decreased postoperatively.

options.text: Right to left shunt from intracardiac defect forming acutely
options.rationale: Wrong because acute intracardiac shunt formation is unlikely postoperatively; this would be correct if a new structural defect were documented.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar flooding causing diffusion block
options.rationale: Wrong because pulmonary edema causes diffusion impairment and low V/Q, not high V/Q; this would be correct if imaging showed bilateral alveolar edema.

options.text: Increased inspired oxygen tension causing absorption atelectasis
options.rationale: Wrong because while high FiO2 can contribute to absorption atelectasis, it does not explain sudden hypoxemia from embolism; this would be correct only if prolonged high FiO2 caused alveolar collapse.

question: A patient with chronic interstitial lung disease has PaO2 = 68 mmHg [>80] and PaCO2 = 36 mmHg [35-45]. The lecture emphasizes DLCO testing. If DLCO is low, which management step is most likely to improve resting PaO2 according to lecture principles?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Administer supplemental oxygen to raise alveolar PO2
options.rationale: Correct because diffusion impairment benefits from increased alveolar PO2 which increases the driving gradient for O2 diffusion across a thickened membrane; the lecture states supplemental oxygen improves hypoxemia in diffusion impairment. If DLCO were normal, oxygen would still help but other causes might be considered.

options.text: Begin high dose systemic corticosteroids immediately
options.rationale: Wrong because steroids may treat inflammatory causes but do not acutely improve diffusion-limited hypoxemia; this would be correct only if an inflammatory, steroid-responsive process were proven.

options.text: Perform immediate lung transplantation to restore DLCO
options.rationale: Wrong because transplantation is definitive but not an immediate management step; this would be correct only as a long-term plan for end-stage disease.

options.text: Start bronchodilator therapy to increase DLCO
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchodilators do not increase DLCO in interstitial disease; this would be correct if reversible airway obstruction were present.

options.text: Induce hypercapnia to shift oxyhemoglobin curve
options.rationale: Wrong because inducing hypercapnia worsens acid-base and does not reliably improve oxygenation; this would be correct only in very specific permissive hypercapnia ventilation strategies unrelated to diffusion correction.

question: A patient with severe COPD has chronic hypoxemia that improves with supplemental oxygen. The lecture differentiates causes. Which physiologic descriptor best matches his condition?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Low ventilation perfusion ratio causing widened A-a gradient
options.rationale: Correct because COPD commonly produces regional low V/Q units that widen the A-a gradient and typically improve with supplemental oxygen, as the lecture describes. If oxygen failed to improve PaO2, a shunt would be more likely.

options.text: Pure diffusion impairment with low DLCO only
options.rationale: Wrong because COPD often has normal DLCO and V/Q mismatch rather than isolated diffusion impairment; this would be correct if DLCO were demonstrably reduced and exercise worsened hypoxemia.

options.text: Global hypoventilation with normal A-a gradient
options.rationale: Wrong because COPD causes regional V/Q mismatch rather than uniform hypoventilation; this would be correct if neuromuscular failure caused global underventilation.

options.text: Anatomic right to left shunt unresponsive to oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because COPD-related hypoxemia usually responds to oxygen; this would be correct if an intracardiac shunt were present.

options.text: High V/Q dead space physiology improving with oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because high V/Q (dead space) does not typically cause hypoxemia that improves with oxygen; this would be correct if perfusion loss predominated without low V/Q regions.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema has PaO2 that improves with oxygen but A-a gradient remains elevated. According to the lecture, which combined mechanism best explains this pattern?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Low V/Q regions from alveolar flooding with partial ventilation
options.rationale: Correct because pulmonary edema creates poorly ventilated but perfused alveoli (low V/Q) that widen the A-a gradient yet still allow some oxygen uptake so supplemental oxygen improves PaO2; the lecture lists pulmonary edema under low V/Q causes. If alveoli were completely collapsed producing true shunt, oxygen would not correct PaO2.

options.text: Pure diffusion block preventing any oxygen transfer
options.rationale: Wrong because pure diffusion block may improve with high FiO2 and is less likely to show improvement if complete; this would be correct only with extreme membrane failure.

options.text: Global hypoventilation causing elevated PaCO2 and normal A-a
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation yields a normal A-a and hypercapnia, not the pattern described; this would be correct if PaCO2 were high.

options.text: Anatomic intracardiac shunt mixing venous blood
options.rationale: Wrong because intracardiac shunt typically shows poor oxygen response; this would be correct if oxygen failed to raise PaO2 despite high FiO2.

options.text: High V/Q dead space physiology from embolism
options.rationale: Wrong because dead space physiology does not usually improve PaO2 with oxygen in the same way and is not caused by alveolar flooding; this would be correct if perfusion loss predominated.

question: A patient with sleep apnea has intermittent nocturnal hypoxemia. The lecture lists sleep apnea under hypoventilation causes. Which daytime ABG pattern would most likely be seen if chronic hypoventilation develops?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Elevated PaCO2 with low PaO2 and normal A-a gradient
options.rationale: Correct because chronic hypoventilation from sleep apnea can lead to daytime hypercapnia and hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient as alveolar ventilation is globally reduced; the lecture groups sleep apnea under hypoventilation causes. If A-a were widened, additional pulmonary pathology would be suspected.

options.text: Low PaCO2 with low PaO2 and widened A-a gradient
options.rationale: Wrong because low PaCO2 indicates hyperventilation or altitude, not chronic hypoventilation; this would be correct if the patient were hyperventilating.

options.text: Normal PaCO2 with low PaO2 and low DLCO
options.rationale: Wrong because low DLCO suggests diffusion impairment rather than hypoventilation; this would be correct if interstitial disease were present.

options.text: Very high PaO2 with low PaCO2 from supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because supplemental oxygen may raise PaO2 but does not reflect the natural daytime ABG pattern of chronic hypoventilation; this would be correct only after oxygen therapy.

options.text: Elevated PaCO2 with very high DLCO and widened A-a
options.rationale: Wrong because DLCO is not typically elevated in hypoventilation and would not explain widened A-a; this would be correct only with measurement error.

question: A patient with severe ARDS has a P/F ratio of 85 and is refractory to oxygen. The lecture suggests shunt physiology predominates. Which immediate ventilatory strategy aligns with correcting the primary problem?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Apply positive end expiratory pressure to recruit alveoli
options.rationale: Correct because PEEP can open collapsed alveoli, reduce intrapulmonary shunt by restoring ventilation to perfused units, and improve PaO2 in ARDS as implied by shunt physiology in the lecture. If alveoli are nonrecruitable, PEEP may have limited benefit.

options.text: Decrease FiO2 to avoid oxygen toxicity immediately
options.rationale: Wrong because lowering FiO2 in severe refractory hypoxemia would worsen oxygenation; this would be correct only after oxygenation improves and FiO2 can be safely reduced.

options.text: Induce permissive hypercapnia to raise PaO2
options.rationale: Wrong because permissive hypercapnia is a ventilatory strategy to limit barotrauma but does not directly raise PaO2; this would be correct only as part of lung-protective ventilation when oxygenation is acceptable.

options.text: Immediate extracorporeal membrane oxygenation without trial
options.rationale: Wrong because ECMO is a rescue therapy but PEEP recruitment is a standard initial step; this would be correct only if maximal conventional measures fail.

options.text: Start inhaled bronchodilators to reduce shunt
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchodilators do not correct alveolar collapse causing shunt; this would be correct only if bronchospasm contributed to V/Q mismatch.

question: A young adult with sarcoidosis has exertional hypoxemia and low DLCO. The lecture links sarcoidosis to diffusion impairment. Which physiologic test result would best support diffusion limitation as the primary cause?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Markedly reduced DLCO with widened A-a gradient at rest
options.rationale: Correct because sarcoidosis thickens the alveolar-capillary membrane reducing DLCO and widening the A-a gradient; the lecture identifies low DLCO and high A-a as hallmarks of diffusion impairment. If DLCO were normal, alternative causes like V/Q mismatch would be more likely.

options.text: Normal DLCO with PaO2 normal and elevated PaCO2
options.rationale: Wrong because normal DLCO and hypercapnia point to hypoventilation rather than diffusion impairment; this would be correct if neuromuscular weakness were present.

options.text: No change in PaO2 with exercise but low resting PaO2
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment typically worsens with exercise causing further desaturation; this would be correct only if exercise did not alter transit time or diffusion gradient.

options.text: Improvement of PaO2 with 100% oxygen minimal
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment usually improves with high FiO2; minimal improvement suggests shunt. This would be correct if oxygen failed to raise PaO2 significantly.

options.text: Normal A-a gradient with low DLCO
options.rationale: Wrong because low DLCO usually accompanies widened A-a; this would be correct only in measurement error or mixed pathologies.

question: A patient with acute massive hemoptysis develops hypoxemia unresponsive to oxygen. The lecture lists intrapulmonary shunt among causes. Which immediate physiologic explanation best fits this scenario?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Airways filled with blood creating perfused but unventilated units
options.rationale: Correct because alveoli filled with blood are perfused but not ventilated, producing true intrapulmonary shunt (V/Q = 0) that mixes venous blood into arterial circulation and resists correction by supplemental oxygen as the lecture explains. If bleeding were minor and ventilation preserved, oxygen might improve PaO2.

options.text: Massive bronchospasm causing reversible low V/Q
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchospasm causes low V/Q that often improves with bronchodilators and oxygen; this would be correct if airway obstruction were the primary issue.

options.text: Global hypoventilation from sedative overdose
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and shows normal A-a gradient; this would be correct if ABG showed hypercapnia.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism causing high V/Q dead space
options.rationale: Wrong because embolism reduces perfusion, not ventilation, and typically does not produce oxygen-unresponsive hypoxemia; this would be correct if imaging confirmed embolus.

options.text: Diffusion impairment from alveolar membrane thickening
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment usually partially improves with high FiO2 and is not caused acutely by hemoptysis; this would be correct if chronic interstitial disease were present.

question: A patient with suspected hypoxemia has ABG showing PaO2 = 55 mmHg [>80], PaCO2 = 80 mmHg [35-45], and PAO2 = 60 mmHg [>100]. The lecture provides a diagnostic approach. Which cause best matches these values?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how A-a O2 gradient, PO2 and PCO2 are used for differentiation of different types of hypoxemia (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Primary hypoventilation producing parallel gas changes
options.rationale: Correct because hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers PAO2 and PaO2 by similar amounts producing a normal A-a gradient, as the lecture demonstrates with numerical examples; the very high PaCO2 here points to hypoventilation. If PaCO2 were low, high altitude would be more likely.

options.text: High altitude exposure with compensatory hyperventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because altitude causes low PaCO2 from hyperventilation, not elevated PaCO2; this would be correct if PaCO2 were low and PAO2 reduced due to low barometric pressure.

options.text: Right to left shunt mixing venous blood into arterial blood
options.rationale: Wrong because shunt typically shows normal or low PaCO2 and a widened A-a gradient; this would be correct if oxygen failed to raise PaO2 despite high FiO2.

options.text: Diffusion impairment with low DLCO and exercise worsening
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment usually does not produce marked hypercapnia at rest; this would be correct if DLCO were low and A-a gradient widened.

options.text: Low V/Q mismatch from localized pneumonia
options.rationale: Wrong because low V/Q often has normal PaCO2 and widened A-a gradient; this would be correct if PaCO2 were normal and oxygen improved PaO2.

question: A patient with severe COPD has chronic hypoxemia and secondary polycythemia. The lecture discusses oxygen content. Which factor most directly increases arterial oxygen content when supplemental oxygen is given?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the main causes of hypoxemia: high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, pulmonary shunt, ventilation/perfusion mismatch (AACOM I.2. b; Il.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 - 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increase dissolved oxygen and hemoglobin saturation
options.rationale: Correct because supplemental oxygen raises PAO2, increasing dissolved O2 and shifting hemoglobin toward full saturation, thereby increasing total oxygen content as the lecture's admixture examples show. If hemoglobin were severely low, oxygen content would still be limited despite saturation.

options.text: Increase hemoglobin concentration acutely without transfusion
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen therapy does not acutely change hemoglobin mass; this would be correct only after transfusion or erythropoiesis over time.

options.text: Decrease cardiac output to raise arterial oxygen tension
options.rationale: Wrong because lowering cardiac output does not increase arterial oxygen content and may worsen tissue delivery; this would be correct only in specific hemodynamic manipulations not recommended for oxygenation.

options.text: Increase mixed venous oxygen content by reducing extraction
options.rationale: Wrong because supplemental oxygen primarily affects arterial oxygen content; increasing mixed venous O2 would require reducing tissue extraction, not immediate oxygen therapy. This would be correct only if tissue metabolism changed.

options.text: Shift oxyhemoglobin curve left by inducing alkalosis
options.rationale: Wrong because shifting the curve left increases saturation at a given PaO2 but is not the primary mechanism of supplemental oxygen; this would be correct only if pH changes occurred and affected affinity.
